senses: A frater house.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin frāter (“brother”). Doublet of bhai, brother, bru, friar, pal, and vai.

senses: To treat a container with resin, e.g. by impregnation in order to impart flavour, typically of wine, and to provide a tighter seal on the container.
examples: Pitch could be used to resinate wine barrels (4.6.2), among other things.

senses: A Japanese family crest
The first principle of metals, that is, mercury, which was formerly supposed to exist in all metals, and to be extractable from them.
The universal remedy of Paracelsus.
ety: From Andalusian Arabic الزُّوق (az-zūq), from Arabic الزَّاوُوق (az-zāwūq, “quicksilver”). Not related to azote.

senses: Any amphibian of the order Anura: any frog (narrow sense) or toad.
ety: From New Latin Anoura, Anura (“name of the order of amphibians”), or from French Anoures (“name of a family of amphibians”), from Ancient Greek ἀν- (an-, “lacking”)) + Ancient Greek οὐρά (ourá, “tail”) + -an.

senses: The official currency of the People's Republic of China.
ety: From the Hanyu Pinyin romanization of Mandarin 人民幣／人民币 (rénmínbì, “people's currency”).

senses: A coarse, loose-textured bobbin lace.
Acanthocybium solandri, a tropical and subtropical game fish.
ety: Perhaps from Wahoo, an obsolete spelling of Oahu, where the fish is found.

senses: A Roman symbol of judicial authority consisting of a bundle of wooden sticks, with an axe blade embedded in the centre; used also as a symbol of fascism.
ety: Borrowed from Latin fascēs (plural of fascis).

senses: A feather-like ornament projecting from a tied turban.
examples: The most ornate and flashy piece of clothing was the turban. It was red in colour with a might turra of gold thread.
Having earlier met Malik Nur Khan, and his tall, wiry father with in his black sherwani and white turban with a turra enhancing his height, I was somewhat more reassured.
A headman of a village, called a Chaudhary or a Malik, would wear a Turra or a ridge on his turban.

senses: A southern African antelope, Tragelaphus angasii (syn. Nyala angasii), with thin white stripes in the grey or brown coat, a ridge of tufted hair running all along the spine, and long horns with a spiral twist.
ety: Probably borrowed from Tsonga nyala. The alternative form inyala is from Zulu inyala.

senses: To fan; to clean grain with a fan.
Capable of being stretched; ductile.
ety: From Latin tēnsilis, from tendō (“to stretch”).

senses: A traditional portable chest from Japan.
The area of Murcia and Valencia with fertile ground.
examples: The city was situated in the huerta, some fifty square miles of rich alluvial fields with extensive irrigation canals, and was bordered by coastal lands dominated by marjals.

senses: A ritual of sacrifice to the Devas.
ety: Borrowed from Sanskrit यज्ञ (yajñá). Doublet of Yasna.

senses: To grow late; become later.
examples: The afternoon was latening, but there was, I think, a quietly commemorative glow from the west.

Not even when the hour latened, when the courts became filled with boys returning from their holidays, when the moment for saying "Good-bye" was only a few minutes distant, not even then did his high spirits leave him.
Then he returned to Margaret's side and sat with her for the rest of the evening, insisting that she rest. As the hour latened he kissed her on the cheek and got up to leave.

senses: An unfiltered type of wheat beer.
A subdivision of currency, equal to one hundredth of a pula.
The quality of being manoeuvrable; ability to be manoeuvred.
Ability to manoeuvre; ability to carry out a manoeuvre or strategic plan.
examples: Articulated buses were invented to improve the manoeuvrability of long buses capable of carrying a large number of passengers.
She became disrespectfully referred to locally as the "Crab" on account of her extraordinary manoeuvrability.
My manoeuvrability is limited. I don't have many options left.

senses: Just arrived; lately come.
ety: From Middle English neowecomen, from Old English nīwcumen, nīwancumen (“newly come, just arrived”), equivalent to new- + come.

senses: Somewhat big.
Any healthcare practitioner working at the point of care, in clinical practice (e.g., physicians in clinical medicine, nurses in nursing practice, or allied health providers in practice).
ety: From French clinicien, equivalent to clinic + -ian.

senses: A machine that reduces solids to small pieces.
Tarry oil of European white birch, formerly used in the arts and in medicine.
A unique example or specimen of something
ety: From the Latin ūnicum, the neuter nominative singular form of ūnicus (“unique”). Compare Dutch unicum, German Unicum. See unique.

senses: A similar rotational bearing used in automotive suspensions.
A female guajiro.
A style of rural Cuban music.
A bootmaker's tool for crimping boot fronts.
ety: From Middle English flowndre, from Anglo-Norman floundre, from Old Northern French flondre, from Old Norse flyðra, from Proto-Germanic *flunþrijǭ. Cognate with Danish flynder, German Flunder, Swedish flundra.

senses: To renovate an old building or structure in a lavish and expensive, yet tasteless fashion which spoils its original beauty.
ety: In reference to the renovation of the St Albans Cathedral in the 19th century by Edmund Beckett, 1st Baron Grimthorpe, which was fiercely criticized at the time.

senses: Synonym of quadrirotor (“having four rotors or four main rotors”).
gallant and respectful, especially to women
A reddish-brown color, like that of polished copper.
A pint of milk.
ety: From the pronunciation of pint of milk. Compare cuppa.

senses: The act of removing duplication or redundancy.
Shaped like the letter delta (Δ), or like an equiangular or equilateral triangle.
A measure of land in India, varying from a third of an acre to an acre.
A homecoming, as after a long journey.
Made without meat (and thus permitted to be eaten on a fast day).
Belonging to a fast day or fast.
ety: Borrowed from French maigre. Doublet of meager.

senses: Suffering from hypochondria.
